content.text:
**The biggest build-time difference is Clang versus GCC, especially when optimizing the large generated kernels.** The Mac workflow also does less work overall.

I compared [your Ubuntu run](https://github.com/Maxwell-Rosen/gkeyll/actions/runs/36265952125) with [the Mac job](https://github.com/gkeyllorg/gkeyll/actions/runs/36207874442/job/108308132178):

| | Ubuntu | Mac |
|---|---|---|
| Compiler | GCC 13.3 | Apple Clang 21 |
| Parallelism | `-j 4` | `-j 3` |
| Optimization | `-O3 -g -ffast-math` | Same |
| Vlasov build | 19m 47s | 12m 47s |
| Gyrokinetic build | 12m 23s | 3m 23s |

The Mac timings **include compiling unit tests**, whereas those Ubuntu timings cover library build/install. Both compile exactly **1,641 Vlasov source files**. Mac is doing comparable compilation work with fewer parallel jobs.

To isolate compiler choice from hardware, I compiled one large Vlasov kernel on this laptop using identical flags:

- **Clang 21:** 12.3 seconds.
- **GCC 15:** exceeded the 120-second limit.

That is one kernel, using different compiler versions from CI—not a whole-build speedup estimate. Nevertheless, it demonstrates that GCC’s optimization cost can dominate even on the same hardware. Your laptop already uses Clang. Apple Silicon versus the Ubuntu runner’s x86 hardware also contributes, but these runs cannot isolate that effect.

The Mac job’s shorter **total duration** has another explanation: it builds libraries and test executables, but does **not run the unit tests, Valgrind checks, or baseline regression comparison**. It also uses Apple’s Accelerate library and spends only 34 seconds preparing SuperLU. Ubuntu spends 6m 56s preparing dependencies.

For acceleration, I recommend this order:

1. **Trial Clang in Ubuntu CI, retaining `-O3`.** This is the most promising small change for clean builds. Compare build times and test results; retain GCC coverage in a separate periodic job.
2. **Add persistent `ccache`.** This should avoid recompiling unchanged generated kernels on subsequent runs. Normalize paths between candidate and baseline, and restrict changing build-date/revision definitions to files that actually use them to improve direct cache hits. [ccache documentation](https://ccache.dev/manual/4.12.2.html)
3. **Cache installed dependencies.** This targets much of the nearly seven-minute preparation stage. Key the cache on platform, toolchain, and dependency versions/build options. [GitHub caching documentation](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/dependency-caching)
4. **Reuse cached compilation for the baseline build.** The regression stage currently starts another clean build; it should benefit from the same compiler cache.
5. **Consider larger runners afterward.** Ubuntu already uses all four available CPUs. Increasing `-j` alone does not address expensive individual compilations.

I would prioritize **Clang plus caching**, preserving optimization and test coverage. No repository files were changed.
